endings.text:
End of the walk at 2100 Prairie. These seven houses are a sketchbook of the architects who rebuilt Chicago after the fire. A few years from now Burnham will take the lesson from this street to the whole city: his 1909 Plan of Chicago, 'the first comprehensive plan for the controlled growth of an American city'.

Look for their other fronts as you explore. Every one of them is signed in stone.

evidence.locator: The page's history of the street, the paragraph on its architects.
evidence.text: Burnham & Root received nearly a dozen commissions on the street, beginning with the John Sherman house at 2100 S. Prairie.
Marshall Field Sr. residence at 1905 S. Prairie.

evidence.locator: The page's history of the street, the paragraphs on its first great houses and its architects.
evidence.text: Richard Morris Hunt of New York and Henry Hobson Richardson of Boston were engaged to design the Marshall Field house and another; George Pullman and Marshall Field both acquired property on the street.

evidence.locator: HABS Part I.A.2, date of erection, data page 2; the museum biography's paragraph on his death.
evidence.text: HABS dates the building from June 1, 1886 to December 1, 1887; the house museum gives Richardson's death as April 26, 1886.
John Glessner Residence. Built 1887; Henry Hobson Richardson, architect. Designed in the Richardsonian Romanesque style, the house is wrapped around a spacious light-filled courtyard.
The district draft reads the Hibbard house from the T-1837 register as an Italianate mansion with a rear addition: a low hip on bracketed eaves over a stone-based body, and the 1874 rear range.

evidence.locator: The 1701 S. Prairie Avenue entry: its name line, and its description as read in paraphrase.
evidence.text: William G. Hibbard Residence. Built 1869; William Le Baron Jenney, architect; Hibbard was president of a large wholesale hardware firm (read in paraphrase).

evidence.locator: Printed p. 28, right column near foot, paragraph beginning Architects Cobb & Frost report.
evidence.text: For O. R. Keith, three story dwelling, 38 by 80 feet, 1808 Prairie avenue, granite front; cost $40,000.
William W. Kimball Residence. Built 1890; Solon S. Beman, architect. Built for the prominent Chicago piano and organ manufacturer in the French Chateauesque style.

evidence.locator: The 1729 S. Prairie Avenue entry: its name line, and its description as read in paraphrase.
evidence.text: The district marker names George M. Pullman Residence, built 1870-1876, Henry S. Jaffay architect, and (read in paraphrase) a theatre of about 200 seats, a pipe organ and a bowling alley, with later additions by Solon S. Beman including a palm room and a large conservatory.

John B. Sherman Residence. Built 1874; Burnham & Root, architects. Sherman was manager of the Union Stock Yards; his daughter Margaret married the architect Daniel Burnham during construction, and Sherman often recommended the firm to his neighbors, making them the most prolific architects represented on the street.
The route, its order, its autumn afternoon, its reading times, its keepsake and its framing are modern interpretation; no historical visit, conversation or occupant on a day in 1904 is asserted.
George H. Wheeler Residence. Built 1884; Burnham & Root, architects. A picturesque brick row house in the Dutch vernacular style.

evidence.locator: The whole print: the street front of 1812 from the walk to the gable's finial.
evidence.text: Albert Levy's photograph shows the front carried up as a tall shaped (Flemish) gable over brick upper storeys and a stone first storey.
Glessner remembered Richardson weighing three hundred and seventy pounds: 'big-minded, big-bodied, big-hearted'.

Three weeks before his death, too ill to leave his bedroom, Richardson marked the places for the lighting fixtures and said: 'There, Mr. Glessner if I were to live five years longer, that is the last thing I would do on your house, my part is finished.' Glessner was convinced it was the house Richardson would most have liked to live in himself.
Norcross Brothers of Worcester, Massachusetts, built the house for the contract price, with no bill of extras.
George Pullman, across the street, complained of the Glessner house: 'I do not know what I have ever done to have that thing staring me in the face every time I go out of my door'.

evidence.locator: The paragraphs on the Home Insurance Building and his office.
evidence.text: Of Jenney's Home Insurance Building, 1884-1885: 'The building was the first fully metal-framed building and is considered the first skyscraper'; Louis Sullivan, Daniel Burnham, William Holabird and Martin Roche 'performed their architectural apprenticeships on Jenney's staff'.
In 1879 Solon S. Beman, born in 1853, 'received a commission from George Pullman to design what would become the nation's first planned company town'; he designed several buildings for the 1893 fair.

Burnham: 'Make no little plans. They have no magic to stir men's blood and probably will not themselves be realized.' He was Director of Works of the 1893 fair, the 'White City', and co-wrote the 1909 Plan of Chicago; in 1876 he married Margaret, daughter of John B. Sherman.

'Hunt was the first American to be admitted to the school of architecture at the École des Beaux-Arts'; his works include 'the pedestal of the Statue of Liberty' and Biltmore, 'America's largest private house'.
Joseph G. Coleman Residence. Built 1886; Cobb & Frost, architects. Cobb & Frost were well known for their designs in the Romanesque style, executed here in rough-faced brown sandstone.
Burnham and Edward H. Bennett's 1909 Plan of Chicago, 'the first comprehensive plan for the controlled growth of an American city'.

William G. Hibbard Residence, 1701 S. Prairie Avenue: in 1921 the house was bought by the American Terra Cotta & Ceramic Co., which gave the architect Louis Sullivan free office space there until his death in 1924. Razed 1932.
Osborn R. Keith Residence, 1808 S. Prairie Avenue: the north wall was retained during demolition in 1968 to preserve the private courtyard of the adjacent Glessner house.
George H. Wheeler Residence, 1812 S. Prairie Avenue: razed 1968.
Marshall Field Residence, 1905 S. Prairie Avenue: later converted to an aeronautical university. Razed 1955.
John B. Sherman Residence, 2100 S. Prairie Avenue: razed 1936.

opening.text:
JAUNT: ARCHITECTS. An autumn afternoon on Prairie Avenue, 1904, the low sun raking across stone. Thirty-three years ago Chicago burned; it rebuilt itself as a daring new city, and many of the architects who did it built houses on this street, for clients who could pay for anything.

Seven houses on foot, 1701 to 2100 Prairie: the man who built the first skyscraper, a giant from Boston, the firm of Cobb and Frost, the young Burnham and Root, the designer of a whole company town, the architect of the Statue of Liberty's pedestal, and the house that started it all for Daniel Burnham. He married the client's daughter.

Begin at 1701, with a modest Italianate front by a very immodest engineer.

armour_corwith_house_1945_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Mrs. Henry Corwith here. Before them, the Armour household lived here (1890-1891).

armour_house_2115_prairie.text: A stone house with a steep mansard roof, built for the lumberman David Kelley. The family of the meatpacker Philip D. Armour lived here for nearly 50 years. Armour's widow was one of the last people living on the street.

buckingham_house_2036_prairie.text: Clarence Buckingham's house in the 1904 Blue Book. In 1927 his sister Kate will give Chicago the Buckingham Fountain in his memory, its centre jet throwing water 150 feet up.

coleman_ames_house_1811_prairie.text: A Romanesque house of rough brown sandstone, built in 1886 for Joseph G. Coleman. Cobb and Frost were the architects. It still stands.

dent_house_1823_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Thomas Dent here, a lawyer by the 1900 census.

dexter_house_1721_prairie.text: Wirt Dexter's house of 1863, given a new front by Arthur Little in 1889. By 1904 the Blue Book lists Henry H. Walker here.

edson_keith_house_1906_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Mrs. Edson Keith here.

elbridge_keith_house_1900_prairie.text: A limestone house with a steep slate roof, built for Elbridge Keith, a hat merchant who became a banker. The top floor inside that roof was added in the 1880s. It is the last Second Empire house left on Prairie Avenue.

fort_dearborn_massacre_monument_1893.text: A bronze group by Carl Rohl-Smith, paid for by George M. Pullman and set up beside his house in 1893. It shows the Potawatomi leader Black Partridge saving Margaret Helm during the battle of August 1812.

george_glessner_house_1706_prairie.text: Home of George M. Glessner, son of the granite house at 1800; the Glessners built it beside his sister's house at 1700.

glessner_house.text: A granite fortress on the street, with a sunny courtyard inside. People passing by remarked on its narrow windows along 18th Street, not knowing the big ones face the courtyard. By 1904 John and Frances Glessner had lived here since 1887.

glessner_lee_house_1700_prairie.text: Built by the Glessners for their daughter Frances, who married Blewett Lee in 1898. Decades on she will build the Nutshell Studies of Unexplained Death, tiny crime scenes still used to train investigators.

goodman_house_1612_prairie.text: Joseph Goodman's stone Italianate of 1869, two years before the Great Fire: round-headed windows under long keystones, and an arched portico at the top of a high stoop.

henderson_house_1816_prairie.text: In 1904 the Blue Book lists Mrs. Charles M. Henderson here. Before them, W. H. Merrill jr. lived here (1899-1903).

premise: An autumn afternoon with the architects who rebuilt Chicago: Jenney, Richardson, Cobb & Frost, Burnham & Root, Beman and Hunt, ending where Burnham met his wife.

stops.text: 1701 Prairie, William G. Hibbard's house of 1869, for the president of a big wholesale hardware firm. Its architect, William Le Baron Jenney, trained as an engineer, and fifteen years after this house he built the Home Insurance Building downtown: 'The building was the first fully metal-framed building and is considered the first skyscraper'. His drafting room was the school of a generation: Louis Sullivan, Daniel Burnham, William Holabird and Martin Roche 'performed their architectural apprenticeships on Jenney's staff'. Here he gave Hibbard a sober Italianate, a low hipped roof on bracketed eaves. The house will end with a fitting tenant: from 1921 its owners give Sullivan a free office here until his death in 1924, and in 1932 it is razed. South to the corner, and a very different kind of genius.

1800 Prairie, Henry Hobson Richardson's house for John J. Glessner. Glessner remembered his architect weighing 370 pounds: 'big-minded, big-bodied, big-hearted'. Three weeks before he died, too ill to leave his bedroom, Richardson marked where the lights would go and said, 'There, Mr. Glessner if I were to live five years longer, that is the last thing I would do on your house, my part is finished.' He died on 26 April 1886; building began on 1 June, and Norcross Brothers built it for the contract price, not a dollar more. The neighbours were appalled. George Pullman grumbled about 'that thing staring me in the face'. Now look next door.

1808 Prairie, next door, by Cobb and Frost for Osborn R. Keith. The notice of 1886 reads like a price tag: a three-storey dwelling, 38 by 80 feet, with a granite front, at a cost of forty thousand dollars. This house went up the same year Richardson's drawings next door were being built, granite answering granite. When it is razed in 1968, its north wall will be left standing to keep the Glessner courtyard private. Two doors south is the firm that would outbuild them all.

1812 Prairie, George H. Wheeler's house of 1884 by Burnham and Root: a picturesque brick row house in the Dutch manner, its front carried up as a tall shaped gable over a stone first storey. It will be razed in 1968. Within a decade Burnham would run the building of the 1893 World's Fair, the 'White City'. His motto: 'Make no little plans. They have no magic to stir men's blood and probably will not themselves be realized.' Cross the avenue to a chateau by a man who once planned an entire town.

1801 Prairie, Solon S. Beman's chateau of 1890 for the piano maker William W. Kimball, French Chateauesque, steep slate and a round tower. Beman was in his twenties when he 'received a commission from George Pullman to design what would become the nation's first planned company town', Pullman, south of the city. He also added the palm room and conservatory to Pullman's own house up the street. Walk south to the street's most famous name, and the most famous architect.

1905 Prairie, Marshall Field's house, by Richard Morris Hunt of New York. 'Hunt was the first American to be admitted to the school of architecture at the École des Beaux-Arts' in Paris, and he designed 'the pedestal of the Statue of Liberty' and Biltmore, 'America's largest private house'. For Chicago's richest man he built a broad brick and stone mansion under a mansard; it ends as an aeronautical university and is razed in 1955. One more stop, at 2100, where a young architect met his wife.

2100 Prairie, John B. Sherman's house of 1874, the first of nearly a dozen Burnham and Root commissions on this street. Sherman ran the Union Stock Yards. While the house was going up, his daughter Margaret married the young architect Daniel Burnham, in 1876, and Sherman started telling his neighbours whom to hire. That is how a firm gets a street: the client becomes your father-in-law, and the father-in-law becomes your salesman. Burnham and Root became the most prolific architects on Prairie Avenue. The house where it started is razed in 1936.

title: Architects of Prairie Avenue
